Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Violence: Violence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Nadia is a fifty-nine-year-old Middle Eastern American police officer. The assault that reshaped her life happened twelve years ago, when she was forty-seven and twelve years into her career in a mid-sized city. She had responded to a disturbance call alone because her partner was tied up elsewhere—a decision that later felt like a setup, though she knew it was just bad luck. The suspect, a large man high on meth, had seemed compliant at first, then lunged before she could radio for backup. He pinned her against the patrol car, one hand around her throat, the other fumbling for her duty belt. She remembered the sound of his breathing—raspy, wet—and the grinding of gravel under her back as she struggled. She managed to draw her Taser, but not before he squeezed hard enough that she saw black spots. By the time backup arrived, he had fled. Nadia was left with a bruised trachea and a citation for failing to secure the scene.

In the years that followed, her body seemed to hold a grudge. A sudden startle—a car backfiring, a door slamming—would flood her with adrenaline, her heart slamming against her ribs so hard that she felt it in her teeth. That pounding became its own threat. She had come to believe that her body was betraying her, that the racing heart was a sign she was about to lose control or, worse, that the attack was happening again. When she was alone and her heart beat fast from climbing stairs or from a nightmare, she would freeze, certain that the terror was proof she was still in danger. She began to monitor her own thoughts obsessively, scanning for any hint of the memory intruding, because if it came unbidden, she was convinced that meant she was cracking up. The thought itself felt like evidence of insanity. This internal vigilance exhausted her, and she sometimes wondered if her Middle Eastern heritage made her more ashamed of seeking help—her family valued strength and self-reliance, and admitting she was struggling felt like dishonoring that.

Memories of the assault were not vague. They arrived as complete sensory episodes: the pressure on her throat, the smell of sweat and chemical residue, and most disturbingly, the sound—that wet, labored breathing in her ears, as if he were still there, whispering. Remembering brought the same raw terror, a full-body clench that left her drenched and shaking. She could see every detail of the gravel, the sky, the buttons on his shirt. There was no fading; twelve years had not blurred a single edge.

Her response to the world outside was systematic. She stopped driving with anyone in the car, even her husband of now thirty years. She told him it was because she needed to concentrate, but the truth was that every passenger became a potential threat: a sudden movement, an angry tone, even a hand reaching for the glove box could trigger the feeling of the chokehold. At work, she avoided riding with her usual partner, requesting solo shifts until the sergeant questioned her reliability. She had always trusted her instincts on the street, but now every person she passed was a person who could attack. She scanned crowds for dangerous faces, for the particular tilt of a head that reminded her of that man. Her hypervigilance was exhausting, but stopping it felt like inviting another assault.

So she withdrew. She stopped answering calls from her sister, declined invitations to family dinners, told her aging mother she was too busy. She had come to believe that she could not rely on anyone—not on the system, which had not arrested the man, and not on people, who were all, in her mind, potential threats. The injustice of it burned: nothing had been done, no one had been held accountable, and she was left carrying the whole thing. The world had shown its true face, and she saw it everywhere now. Her husband tried to reach her, but she would not let him in the car, would not let him touch her when she woke gasping from a nightmare. She slept in a separate room to avoid having to explain why her heart pounded when he turned over in bed.

What finally brought her to the clinic, at age fifty-nine, was a near-collision on the freeway. She had been driving alone, her heart already racing from a news report about a violent assault, when a truck swerved into her lane. She slammed the brakes, and for a moment, she was back on the gravel, the breath leaving her. She pulled over and sat for twenty minutes, unable to move, listening to her own pulse. Afterwards, she called her department’s employee assistance line. She is terrified that she is going crazy, that the monitoring of her thoughts is proof of something broken inside. But she is also exhausted, and somewhere beneath the fear is a fragile hope that maybe, if she talks about it, the sound of his breathing will stop echoing in her head.
